description: Hi, I'm Ana! I'm studying Aerospace Engineering at TU Delft, with a real love for math, physics, and figuring out how things work. I've led teams to a few competition wins along the way, and I'm also part of ROSPIN, a space-industry community. Excited to bring some energy and organization to the team!

details:
Abstract

Heat and vegetation loss affect more people in cities than anywhere else, yet many municipalities cannot easily measure where these conditions are changing, by how much, and whether the changes are significant. As our answer to the Earth System Trend Detective challenge, we present GalacTech, a free, browser-based Google Earth Engine tool that turns NASA's Landsat 8 and 9 observations (2014-2026) into maps and trends for any city, region or custom area. It maps vegetation (NDVI) and land-surface temperature, measures urban heat island intensity against an elevation-matched rural baseline, shows change maps between any two years, and tests each yearly trend with the Mann-Kendall test and Sen's slope. Results are cross-checked with MODIS land-surface temperature (same quantity, different sensor) and ERA5-Land air temperature (an independent reanalysis) to confirm that changes reflect real conditions, not processing artefacts. The tool also estimates how many residents live in strongly heated areas and how much green space each has. It shows what is changing, where, by how much and how reliably, helping planners and citizens decide where to plant trees, set green-space targets and check whether policies work, reducing heat exposure.

Keywords: Landsat 8/9, NDVI, land-surface temperature, urban heat island, trend detection, Google Earth Engine, urban planning, population exposure

1. Introduction

1.1 Motivation

Heat exposure and urban green space are increasingly the subject of local policy, but the satellite record that could guide that policy is hard for non-specialists to use. Choosing variables, removing clouds, building consistent baselines and checking whether a change is real all demand expertise that most municipalities, NGOs and schools do not have. Our aim is to package that workflow so that anyone can run the same transparent analysis for their own area, and so that results from different places can be compared fairly.

1.2 Why cities, and why NDVI and surface temperature

Cities are where a large share of people live and where land-cover change is fastest. Two variables capture much of what changes there:

  • Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), derived from near-infrared and red reflectance, which tracks vegetation cover and vigour.
  • Land-surface temperature (LST), derived from the Landsat thermal infrared band, which shows how strongly surfaces heat up.

Together they connect a cause (loss or gain of vegetation and impervious surface) with a consequence (heat stress, energy demand for cooling, health risk). The difference between urban and rural LST is the urban heat island (UHI) intensity, which is the quantity planners can act on.

1.3 Our approach

Our approach is to build one general tool instead of a study of a single place. A single case cannot reveal general rules, so GalacTech applies exactly the same method to any area: the same satellite record, the same cloud masking, the same fixed urban reference, the same rural baseline, the same trend test and the same cross-checks. This is what makes results comparable between cities and over time. The question we ask is not "what happened in one city?" but how can this kind of data, produced the same way everywhere, inform urbanism and administrative decisions in any place? This report explains how the method works, how far its results can be trusted, how they can be used, and what their limits are.

2. What the Tool Does and How It Works

2.1 Overview of the application

GalacTech is written in the GEE JavaScript API and runs entirely in the Code Editor with no installation. The user works in three steps:

  1. Choose an area. Either type a city name (a built-in list of about 380 major cities, each with a default analysis radius), or select a country -> region -> municipality using administrative boundaries, or enter coordinates or click the map and set a radius of 1-100 km.
  2. Choose a year and a layer. Layers are NDVI, UHI classes, NDVI change and UHI change. Change layers compare a second year with the selected year.
  3. Analyse. Buttons compute statistics for one year, a full 2014-2026 trend analysis with validation, and downloadable GeoTIFF and CSV outputs.

Figure 1. GalacTech interactive interface in Google Earth Engine. The left panel guides users through area selection (shown here for Berlin, DE with a 20 km radius), year and layer selection (2025 Urban Heat Island classes), and statistical analysis, while displaying scene counts (22 scenes) and the rural reference temperature (29.6 °C)

2.2 Satellite data

We use the Landsat Collection 2 Level 2 surface reflectance and surface temperature products of Landsat 8 (OLI/TIRS) and Landsat 9 (OLI-2/TIRS-2). The two satellites carry very similar sensors and operate on a 16-day revisit cycle, providing consistent multispectral and thermal observations across the summer season. The analysis starts in 2014, the first full year of Landsat 8 data, and runs to 2026.

For each year the tool:

  • selects scenes in a fixed seasonal window (default June-September, to compare like with like and to capture the period of greatest heat stress);
  • drops scenes with more than 30 % cloud cover and then masks cloud, cloud shadow, cirrus, snow and fill pixel by pixel using the quality band;
  • computes NDVI from the near-infrared (band 5) and red (band 4) surface reflectance after applying the official scale factors;
  • converts the thermal band (band 10) to LST in kelvin using the official scale factors;
  • builds a median composite, which suppresses residual clouds and outliers, at an analysis scale of 100 m.

The number of scenes used in every composite is displayed, and a warning appears when fewer than three scenes are available, so that users know when to be cautious.

2.3 Fixed urban mask

When the urban mask changes from year to year, an apparent trend can be an artefact of the mask rather than of the environment. To avoid this, the tool uses one fixed land-cover reference for all years: ESA WorldCover 2021 by default, or alternatively the Dynamic World mode over 2020-2025. Trends of urban UHI are therefore trends of surface temperature within the same footprint. The price of this choice is that urban expansion after the reference period is not captured by the mask; we state this openly as a limitation (Section 6).

2.4 Rural reference and UHI intensity

UHI intensity is defined as:

Rural reference pixels must be (a) not built-up, (b) not water, (c) within +/-100 m of the mean elevation of the urban pixels, and (d) inside the analysis area plus a 10 km buffer. The elevation condition avoids a common error in which a city in a valley is compared to cooler hills, which would exaggerate the heat island. Delta T is split into six classes (below 0 °C, 0-2, 2-4, 4-6, 6-8 and 8 °C or more), and a value of 4 °C or more is called a strong UHI. The rural reference temperature of every year is displayed so that users can see the baseline, not only the anomaly.

2.5 Statistics for a selected year

For one year the tool reports:

  • Population exposure. Using the GHSL GHS-POP R2023A population grid (the epoch closest to the selected year: 2015, 2020 or 2025, where 2025 is a projection), it sums the number of residents living in built-up pixels of each UHI class, and the number and percentage living in strong UHI.
  • Green space. The area with NDVI above 0.5, and the green area per resident.
  • NDVI versus Delta T. A sample of up to 1500 pixels (water excluded) is plotted as a scatter plot with a trendline, and the Pearson correlation coefficient is reported. A negative value means greener pixels are cooler.

2.6 Trend analysis 2014-2026

The trend function processes each year separately, which makes the analysis robust (one failing year does not stop the others) and shows progress. For each year it records mean NDVI, mean urban Delta T, mean LST, the rural reference temperature, the number of scenes, and two independent comparison datasets (Section 2.7). It then draws:

  • a chart of mean NDVI and mean urban Delta T over time;
  • a linear trend for each, reported as slope per year, R^2 and number of years used;
  • the correlation between yearly NDVI and yearly urban Delta T;
  • a CSV table of all yearly values for further analysis.

Trend significance. Each yearly series is tested with the Mann-Kendall test, a non-parametric test that asks whether values move consistently up or down over time, without assuming a normal distribution and without being thrown off by single outliers. The tool reports the p-value and a verdict at the 95 % level (significant increase, significant decrease, or no significant trend), together with Sen's slope, the median of all pairwise yearly slopes, which is a robust estimate of how fast the variable changes. The ordinary least-squares slope and R^2 are shown alongside for comparison, and the test results can be downloaded as a CSV table. The test assumes independent yearly values and uses a normal approximation, so with a record of at most 13 years the verdict is indicative, not proof of a long-term climate signal.

Change maps (NDVI change and UHI change between two chosen years) answer the where question: they show which neighbourhoods became greener or hotter, and which did the opposite.

2.7 Cross-checks with independent datasets

A tool that shows temperatures must show that they can be trusted. For every year the tool compares the Landsat LST with:

  • MODIS MOD11A1 daytime LST (Terra, similar overpass time of about 10:30 local time), reporting the correlation and the mean bias;
  • ERA5-Land 2 m air temperature (centre point of the area), reporting the year-to-year correlation. LST and air temperature are different quantities, so only the agreement of their variations is meaningful.

Why these two datasets, and what they can and cannot show. Landsat's thermal data come from one instrument, so a result could in principle reflect cloud masking, compositing or sensor effects instead of real conditions. MODIS measures the same quantity (daytime surface temperature) at about the same time of day, but with a different sensor and retrieval method, so if the two agree from year to year, the Landsat series is unlikely to be a processing artefact. ERA5-Land is a model-based reanalysis of 2 m air temperature that assimilates weather observations. It measures something different from surface temperature, so it cannot confirm Landsat's values; it only shows whether hot and cool summers appear in both. Both comparisons are limited by resolution: MODIS is about 1 km and ERA5-Land about 10 km, against about 100 m for Landsat's thermal band, so they can only be compared on area-wide averages and cannot check neighbourhood detail. They are therefore consistency checks, not a replacement for ground measurements from weather stations.

3. What the Tool Reports

4. Benefits and Intended Impact

The value of the tool is that the same outputs can feed several kinds of decisions, in any city, without needing specialist software.

4.1 Finding where to act first

UHI class maps and NDVI-change maps identify the neighbourhoods that are both hot and losing vegetation. Crossing them with population exposure shows where intervention helps the most people. A municipality can therefore rank districts by residents in strong UHI instead of by area alone, which is a fairer and more efficient criterion for investment in trees, shade, green roofs, reflective surfaces or water features.

4.2 Setting measurable targets

Green area per resident and the share of the built-up population in strong UHI are simple indicators that can be written into urban plans, compared between districts or cities, and re-measured every year. Planners can set targets such as a minimum green area per resident or a reduction in the share of residents in the two hottest classes.

4.3 Checking whether policies work

Because the urban mask and the rural baseline are fixed in the same way for every year, the yearly series can be used as a before-and-after test. If a city adds green roofs, parks or cooling corridors in a district, the NDVI-change and Delta T-change maps show whether that district became greener and cooler compared with the rest, and the trend table quantifies the difference.

4.4 Guiding new development

The maps show which land is already thermally stressed and which green patches act as cooling buffers. Planning authorities can use this to avoid building over high-NDVI patches that cool nearby blocks, to require shade and vegetation in new developments on already hot land, and to preserve ecological and cooling connections between inner-city green space and surrounding countryside.

4.5 Heat-risk and public-health management

Identifying areas where many people, particularly the elderly, children and outdoor workers, live in strong UHI helps health and emergency services decide where to place cooling centres, shaded rest points and heat advisories, and which neighbourhoods to prioritise in heat-wave plans.

4.6 Comparing cities fairly

Because the method is identical for every place, cities can be benchmarked against one another and against national or regional averages, for example a municipality against its region. This helps administrations learn from places that cope better with heat, and helps national agencies direct funding to the municipalities with the largest exposed population.

4.7 Equity and accessibility

The tool is free, runs in a browser and requires no data collection by the user. Small municipalities and organisations without GIS departments can obtain evidence of the same type as large cities, and citizens or journalists can independently check the situation in their own area.

4.8 Intended impact

We want GalacTech to change how heat and green space are discussed in local decisions, in three steps. Now: show that a free, open, browser-based tool can give a defensible, comparable picture of vegetation and heat for any area. Next: let municipalities, NGOs, schools and journalists use it to identify priority districts, set measurable green-space targets and check whether measures work, including for reporting needs such as the urban green space and tree canopy targets of the EU Nature Restoration Regulation. Later: help build a shared, transparent evidence base so that different places can learn from each other. We do not claim that the tool alone cools a city; its intended impact is better-informed decisions on where, how much and whether interventions are needed.

5. Illustrative Application

To demonstrate the workflow, the tool can be run on any area; contrasting cities work best (for example a compact southern European city, a rapidly growing city in a hot climate, and a northern city with extensive green space). For each area the procedure is the same:

  1. Select the area by name or boundary.
  2. Draw NDVI and UHI layers for an early year and a recent year (for example 2015 and 2025) and the two change layers.
  3. Run the year statistics for the recent year to obtain exposed population and green area per resident.
  4. Run the 2014-2026 trend analysis and read the NDVI and Delta T trends with their significance verdicts, and the validation results.
  5. Download the GeoTIFF and CSV for use in reports or further analysis.

Link to a demo showcasing how the application works:

Figure 2. Automated trend significance and multi-sensor validation outputs (2014-2026). 1: Time series of mean NDVI and urban ΔT with Mann-Kendall significance tests (α = 0.05), Sen's slope, OLS regression metrics, and annual scene counts. 2: Independent consistency check comparing Landsat daytime LST against MODIS Terra LST and ERA5-Land 2 m air temperature, accompanied by built-in methodological disclosures.

Comparing different areas also illustrates an important point: the same driver, such as regional warming, can produce different signs and sizes of change in different places, depending on land cover, topography and planning.

6. Limitations and Planned Improvements

We consider honest limitations part of the result.

  • Daytime surface temperature only. Landsat measures LST at roughly 10:30 local time. It is not air temperature and says nothing about night-time heat, which is important for human health. ERA5-Land is used only to check year-to-year agreement.
  • Fixed urban mask. Using the same land-cover reference for all years prevents artificial trends but cannot capture urban growth after the reference year. A future version could use a multi-year land-cover series and compare the two approaches.
  • Sampling in time. Only June-September scenes with enough clear pixels are used, and the number of scenes differs between places and years. Composites based on few scenes are more affected by weather: a hot or cool summer can look like a trend. The tool shows the scene count and warns when it is low.
  • Short record. Thirteen yearly values give a limited basis for a trend, and a linear fit with a high R^2 does not prove a long-term climate signal. Trends should be described as observed changes over 2014-2026.
  • Statistical significance. Trends are tested with the Mann-Kendall test and sized with Sen's slope, but the test assumes independent yearly values and uses a normal approximation. With a record of at most 13 years, the verdict is indicative and not proof of a long-term climate signal. A future version could add pixel-level significance maps, so that users can see where the change is statistically significant and not only whether the area-wide average is.
  • Correlation is not causation. The negative correlation between NDVI and Delta T is expected from physical processes (evapotranspiration and shading), but it also reflects other factors such as surface material, building density and soil moisture.
  • Resolution and population data. Analysis is at 100 m (trends at 200 m) while the native resolution is 30 m (thermal about 100 m, resampled). GHS-POP is modelled and updated every five years, and its 2025 epoch is a projection, so population figures are estimates.
  • Possible extensions. Additional NASA variables (for example night-time temperature from other missions, precipitation, soil moisture or aerosol products) could be added to study causes and not only symptoms, and a generic variable selector would let the tool address a broader range of Earth-system questions.

7. Tools, Languages, Hardware and Software

GalacTech was built entirely with free and open resources.

  • Programming language and platform: JavaScript in the Google Earth Engine Code Editor. The Earth Engine API handles all satellite processing in Google's cloud, and its user-interface toolkit provides the panels, dropdowns, map layers, legends and charts. The statistics (correlation, linear regression, Mann-Kendall test, Sen's slope) are written in plain JavaScript and run on the yearly results. We checked these functions on synthetic yearly series (a clear increase, no trend and a clear decrease) before using them.
  • Satellite data: Landsat 8 and 9 Collection 2 Level 2 surface reflectance and surface temperature (USGS/NASA).
  • Other datasets: ESA WorldCover 2021 (and optionally Dynamic World) for urban and water masks; SRTM elevation for the rural baseline; GHSL GHS-POP R2023A for population; MODIS MOD11A1 land-surface temperature and ERA5-Land air temperature for validation; FAO GAUL for administrative boundaries.
  • Licensing and attribution: All datasets are attributed and used within their respective open-data or noncommercial licence terms (such as Google Earth Engine's noncommercial quota and FAO GAUL boundaries), aligning with our Access and Pricing Model.
  • Outputs: GeoTIFF map layers and CSV tables, which open in any GIS or spreadsheet program.
  • Hardware: no special hardware. The tool runs in a web browser on an ordinary computer, because the heavy computation happens in the cloud.

8. How the Project Is Creative

The individual ingredients (NDVI, surface temperature, population grids) are well known. What is new is how we combine them and for whom.

  • From a map to a decision measure. Many tools show where it is hot. GalacTech also counts how many residents live in strongly heated areas and how much green space each has, so districts can be ranked by people affected, not only by area.
  • Detection, location and trust in one place. The same tool shows what changed, where it changed, whether the change is statistically significant, and whether the temperatures agree with independent datasets. These steps are normally spread over separate software and skills.
  • Design choices that protect against false trends. One fixed urban mask for all years, a rural baseline matched in elevation to the city, pixel-level cloud masking, and a visible scene count with a warning when data are thin.
  • Made for non-specialists. A user can type a city name, or pick a country, region or municipality, and get results without installing anything or writing code.
  • Built to be general. The tool applies the same method for any place on Earth, which makes cities directly comparable.

9. Factors Our Team Considered

  • Scientific validity. Landsat gives daytime surface temperature, not air temperature or night-time heat, so we cross-check against MODIS and ERA5-Land and state this limit openly. We fixed the season (June-September), masked clouds, shadows and snow, and used a median composite to reduce weather effects.
  • Fair comparison over time. A changing land-cover map can create fake trends, so the urban mask is the same in every year. A rural baseline in a different landscape would exaggerate the heat island, so rural pixels must be at a similar elevation.
  • Statistical caution. With a short record, one hot summer can look like a trend. We therefore use a significance test, report sample sizes, and say that the result is indicative. We also avoid claiming that correlation proves causation.
  • Usability and access. Different users need different areas, so the tool supports city search, administrative units and custom circles. It is free, runs in a browser, and offers downloads for reports.
  • Performance and reliability. Yearly analysis runs one small request per year, so a failing year does not stop the others, and trends use a coarser scale to stay fast. Areas are limited to a 1-100 km radius for custom circles.
  • Policy relevance. We designed outputs around questions planners and administrations ask: where to act first, whether a measure worked, and how green space and heat exposure change over time.
  • Data limits and ethics. Population grids are modelled estimates (the 2025 epoch is a projection), and the tool uses no personal data. Results should support, not replace, local knowledge and ground measurements.
  • Future growth. We kept the code modular so that new variables, night-time temperature, and pixel-level significance maps can be added later.

10. Conclusion

GalacTech shows that freely available NASA and USGS satellite data can be turned into a general, transparent and repeatable tool for detecting environmental trends in urban areas. By combining NDVI and surface temperature with a consistent urban mask, an elevation-matched rural baseline, population exposure, green-space indicators and independent validation, it answers the questions of what, where and how much is changing, tests whether each yearly trend is statistically significant (Mann-Kendall test with Sen's slope), and provides the quantitative evidence needed to judge whether changes are meaningful. More importantly, it is not tied to one city: any administration, planner or citizen can use it to find the places where heat and loss of vegetation affect the most people, to set and monitor targets, and to check whether adaptation measures actually work. With pixel-level significance maps and additional variables, it can grow into a broader Earth-system trend-monitoring tool.
